source.title: Using OCR Heads to Verbalize Image Semantics
source.authors: Sheridan Feucht; Benno Krojer; S. Wang; Henry Abrahamsen; Byron C. Wallace; David Bau

record.file_problem: The paper text is present; some figure and table text is flattened or garbled.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies whether image-token activations can be decoded into linguistic semantics, including in early layers. It does not measure similarity between independently trained models, cross-modal distance alignment, convergence across seeds, or any trend with model scale or capability.
record.gate_note: The authors argue that image representations contain linguistic information in early layers, but their verbalization-lens readouts are not a test of convergence between models. The paper cites the Platonic Representation Hypothesis in related work; it does not test that hypothesis. OCR ablations, object-confidence and localization results, and activation edits concern other questions.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a verbalization lens from OCR attention heads inside single VLMs and decodes image-token activations into vocabulary space. It never compares representations between independently trained models, between separate vision and language models on paired data, or across seeds, and reports no trend with scale. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis appears only in a related-work citation. 'Alignment with language in early layers' refers to linear decodability within one VLM's backbone, not cross-model convergence. 'Cites_only' fits better than 'discusses', since there is no substantive argument about the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right, with one correction. The authors conclude that OCR-identified attention heads are general verbalization heads: their combined OV matrix (the verbalization lens) reads out semantics of non-text image tokens from layer 0 across four VLMs. The subspace these heads read from is causally usable for editing object concepts, which was shown only for the Qwen3-VL models. They read this as evidence that image representations are aligned with language in early layers.
record.recipe_differences: No method for measuring convergence between independently trained models is tested.

fits_no_version.finding: A verbalization lens built from OCR heads decodes interpretable semantic tokens from image-token activations starting at layer 0, across four VLMs, where the raw logit lens is noisy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within VLMs, image tokens linearly encode language-decodable semantics from the first decoder layer.

fits_no_version.finding: 6 of 11 filter heads in Qwen3-1.7B are among the top 10% of verbalization heads in Qwen3-VL-2B (Appendix C).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Components of a base language model persist and are repurposed after vision fine-tuning.

record.problems: The paper's semantic-readout findings do not measure inter-model representational similarity or convergence, so they cannot establish the claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were included because the OCR ablations, object detection and localization metrics, and activation-editing results do not test representational convergence.

untested.parts: All: no cross-model similarity and no scale trend (the four models of different sizes are not compared for alignment).
All: no separate vision and language models and no paired image-caption alignment metric.
All: no mapping or stitching between models. The pseudo-inverse is an edit within a single model.

All in effect. The Appendix C overlap between filter heads in Qwen3-1.7B and verbalization heads in Qwen3-VL-2B is a base-versus-fine-tuned comparison of the same model, not independently trained models.

record.verdict_notes: Relation was changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': the Platonic Representation Hypothesis appears only in a related-work citation. The early-layer alignment the paper refers to concerns the modality gap within a single VLM, not convergence between independently trained models.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of independently trained models' representations or their alignment across model scale or capability.
No measurement of representation alignment between vision and language models on paired images and captions, or of how such alignment changes with model performance.
No comparison across random initializations, shared features, or shared subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment test between models.
No comparison of recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
No test of how convergence varies with similarity metric, settings, input choice, or out-of-distribution data.
No test of whether cross-model alignment is incomplete, plateaus, or is explained by shared data or objectives.

rows.subject: Qwen3-VL-2B, Qwen3-VL-8B, Molmo2-O-7B, and Llava-Next-34B (reported together for the layer-0 qualitative result)
rows.operation_detail: Applied the verbalization lens to image-token activations and decoded them into vocabulary space.
rows.measure: Whether decoded tokens provide interpretable linguistic or semantic information about image tokens.
rows.baseline: Raw logit lens, described as noisy in early and middle layers.
rows.value: The authors report interpretable semantic readouts from layer 0; examples include labels for image content.
rows.note: This is evidence about linguistic semantic information being decodable from image representations, not about similarity or convergence between models. Figure 20 compares interpretability scores across layers, not representation alignment.
rows.check: This is a within-model decodability readout and the study's own method compared against the logit lens. It measures no alignment between models, so it bears on no version. As a method-comparison row it should arguably be moved out of the result rows into fits_no_version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
